title: Ganache ratios, pouring, piping, and rolling
subtitle: How the cream-to-chocolate ratio determines whether ganache pours, pipes, or sets firm
excerpt: Ganache is cream and chocolate emulsified together. The ratio of cream to chocolate determines the final consistency. A pourable ganache for coating cakes uses equal parts by weight; a pipeable ganache for truffles uses half the amount of cream; a rolled truffle filling uses even less. Dark, milk, and white chocolate each require different ratios because of their varying fat and sugar content.
sourceNotes: Ganache ratios for dark, milk, and white chocolate are based on standard patisserie practice. The variation in ratios accounts for the difference in fat and sugar content between chocolate types.

recipe.freezeNotes: Ganache freezes well in a sealed container for up to 2 months. Defrost overnight at room temperature and re-stir before using.
recipe.batchNotes: Scales linearly. Double or triple as needed.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Ganache keeps in the fridge for 1 week. Bring to room temperature and re-stir before piping or pouring.

glossaryTerms.definition: A smooth mixture of cream and melted chocolate. Used as a glaze, filling, frosting, or truffle base depending on the cream-to-chocolate ratio.

The stable blending of fat (cocoa butter from the chocolate) and water (from the cream) into a smooth, uniform texture. Ganache is an emulsion. Overheating or incorrect technique breaks the emulsion, making the ganache grainy and separated.

Pouring glaze (for coating cakes, drip cakes): 1 part cream to 1 part chocolate by weight. At room temperature this sets to a glossy, barely firm glaze. At 30°C it pours smoothly.
Pipeable frosting (for filling macarons, piping decorations): 1 part cream to 2 parts chocolate. Sets to a soft, spreadable consistency at room temperature.
Truffle filling (for rolling into balls): 1 part cream to 3 parts chocolate. Sets firm at room temperature, pliable enough to roll between cold hands.
Adjusting for milk and white chocolate

Milk chocolate has more sugar and less cocoa, so it sets softer at the same ratio. Reduce the cream by 20 to 25% compared to dark chocolate. For white chocolate, which has no cocoa solids and the highest sugar and fat content, reduce the cream by a third for a pouring glaze and by half for a truffle filling.
Finely chop the chocolate and place in a heatproof bowl.
Bring the cream to a bare simmer over medium heat, bubbles just breaking the surface, not a rolling boil.
Pour the hot cream over the chocolate. Leave for 1 minute without stirring.
Stir from the centre outward in small circles until the ganache is smooth and glossy. If any chocolate pieces remain unmelted, stand the bowl over a pan of just-simmered water and stir until smooth.
A split ganache looks greasy and grainy with the fat separating from the chocolate solids. Whisk in a tablespoon of warm cream or milk in small amounts until it comes back together.
